items.title: Section: Concrete Care for Those Present — Never Abandoning the Sick, Bending One's Own Conduct to Match Theirs, and Holding Known and Unknown in Perfectly Equal Regard

items.zh: 所攝有情縱懷資給，有病無病，終不棄捐；身業語業，無不隨順。若識不識，一切等心；為友為朋，無怨無隙。
items.en: Towards the beings they have gathered in, bodhisattvas open their heart to provide for them, and, whether such beings are sick or well, never once abandon them. Their bodily and verbal conduct is never anything but accommodating. Whether a being is known to them or unknown, they hold an entirely equal mind towards all, becoming a genuine friend and companion, free of enmity and free of estrangement.

items.title: Section: Refuge for the Utterly Unsupported, Careful Speech Even Among Intimates, and Genuine Release From Resentment Towards Those Who Have Actually Wronged You

items.zh: 於無依怙一切有情，隨力隨能作依作怙。不託異門發他憂苦，令彼須臾住不安樂。若有因緣須現談謔，稱理而為，非不稱理。雖遇情交極相親密，年事斯等無乖隔者，亦不共談匪仁言論。終不於他久懷忿恨，設復暫起，不斥其諱。若復為他身語訾辱，或善思擇、或依正法、或省己過而自開解，不譴於他。
items.en: Towards all beings with no support whatsoever, bodhisattvas become their refuge according to their own strength and ability, never inventing some other pretext to provoke that being's own grief and distress, never allowing them to remain unhappy even for a brief moment. Should there be genuine cause to engage in some lighthearted conversation, this is done in a manner fitting to reason, never contrary to reason. Even when encountering the most intimate of friendships, equal in age and standing and free of any estrangement, bodhisattvas never join in unkind conversation. They never harbour long-term resentment towards another; even should some displeasure arise momentarily, they do not rebuke the other over what that person would rather not hear. Should they be insulted by another's body or speech, they resolve the matter either through careful reflection, or through recourse to the true teaching, or through examining their own faults, thereby releasing it inwardly, without reproaching the other.

items.title: Section: A General Principle Closes This Account — Fourteen Tainted Deeds to Avoid, Six Directions to Honour, and Four Bad Friends to Flee From Four Good Ones to Keep

items.zh: 其心安靜而不輕躁，身語意業起必審詳。普能遠離十四垢業，藏隱六方，遠四惡友，攝四善友。
items.en: Their mind settled and tranquil rather than restless and impulsive, whatever bodily, verbal, or mental action arises is invariably undertaken with careful deliberation. They are able to universally avoid fourteen kinds of tainted action; to honour the six directions in their hidden sense; to keep far from the four kinds of bad friend; and to gather in the four kinds of good friend.

items.title: Section: The Fourteen Tainted Deeds in Full — Four Root Wrongs, Four Causes of a Waning Reputation, and Six Ways an Entire Fortune Quietly Bleeds Away

items.zh: 如是一切，應知具如尸佉絡迦契經中說。
items.en: All of this should be understood exactly as stated in the Sigālovāda Sutta. A person should recognise four matters as genuinely burdensome. What are these four? First, delighting in killing; second, delighting in theft; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, delighting in false speech. It is further said: there are four matters that may lead one towards the lower realms. What are these four? First, craving; second, anger; third, delusion; fourth, fear. "Craving, anger, fear, and delusion — whoever possesses these states finds their reputation diminishing day by day, like the moon waning towards darkness." "Towards craving, hatred, fear, and delusion, whoever does not act wrongly finds their reputation growing day by day, like the moon waxing towards fullness." It is further said: there are six harms that dissipate one's wealth and lead towards the lower realms, and these should be recognised. What are these six? First, indulgence in drink and dissipation; second, entering another's chamber at an improper time; third, gambling and dissipation; fourth, excessive fondness for music and entertainment; fifth, bad companionship; sixth, laziness.

items.title: Section: Self-Benefiting Conduct in Present Matters — Fair Livelihood, Lawful Wealth, and Guarding One's Own Precepts With Genuine Shame

items.zh: 或為現法利益事義財位相應，起策具足、守護具足，平等養命。於諸世間工巧業處皆得善巧，無諂無幻，性不誑他。於罪現行深懷慚恥，正行具足，尊重正行、守護正行。
items.en: Whether pursuing matters of present benefit joined with wealth and status, bodhisattvas act only after full deliberation, maintain complete safeguarding of what has been achieved, and sustain their livelihood in fair and balanced measure. In every worldly trade and craft, they achieve genuine skill, free of flattery and free of deceit, their very nature incapable of misleading others. Should wrongdoing actually occur, they feel deep shame, keep their own correct practice fully intact, and hold correct practice in the highest reverence, safeguarding it at every turn.

items.title: Section: Benefiting Others Opens — Perfect Trustworthiness Down to the Last Fraction of a Coin, and Fitting Skilfully Into the World's Own Social Customs

items.zh: 有所寄付，深可倚信。於他財物，無所規度；舉貸他物，終不違捍；分所共財，平等無矯；共知真寶，賣者不識，稱寶酬價，無枉毫釐。於世時務令儀軌範，為益世間，辯正機捷。
items.en: Whatever is entrusted to them can be deeply relied upon; towards another's property, they harbour no scheme whatsoever; having borrowed another's goods, they never renege on the agreement; dividing jointly held wealth, they do so fairly, without deceit; when something is commonly recognised as a genuine treasure but the seller does not realise this, they pay its true, honest price, without shorting even the smallest fraction. In worldly affairs and customary matters, their conduct accords fully with proper form, benefiting the world through speech that is correct and quick-witted.

items.title: Section: Benefiting Others Closes — a Steady Refuge for Whoever Asks, a Ruler Governing by Dharma Rather Than Force, and the Eight Kinds of Noble Speech

items.zh: 於所應作彼彼事中，他正來求，皆為助伴；敦質無動，不託餘緣；善營事業，非為不善。若為帝王，以法治世，不以非法，不好責罰。若御大眾，勸捨惡戒，令修善戒。成就八種賢聖語言。謂於所見，問答言見；於聞、覺、知，問答言知；於所不見，問答不見；於所不聞、不覺、不知，問答不知。
items.en: In whatever matters genuinely call for it, when another comes directly seeking help, bodhisattvas always become their companion in it; remaining honest and unwavering, never inventing some other pretext to decline; skilfully managing their own undertakings, never through unwholesome means. Should they become a ruler, they govern the world through the dharma, never through unlawful means, and take no pleasure in punishment. Should they lead a following, they encourage the abandonment of unwholesome precepts and the cultivation of wholesome ones. They accomplish eight kinds of noble speech: when asked about what they have seen, they answer that they saw it; when asked about what they have heard, sensed, or known, they answer accordingly; when asked about what they have not seen, they answer that they did not see it; when asked about what they have not heard, sensed, or known, they answer accordingly.

items.title: Section: Skill in Worldly Knowledge Closes With a Summary of All It Contains — Fascicle 44 Concludes Here

items.zh: 菩薩成就如是等法，如其世間正所應知，如其世間正所應轉，於彼一切皆如實知。是故名為善知世間。
items.en: Bodhisattvas who accomplish qualities such as these — correctly knowing the world exactly as it should genuinely be known, and correctly enacting conduct within the world exactly as it should genuinely be enacted — correctly and thoroughly know all of this without exception. For this reason, this is called skill in worldly knowledge.

blocks.text: How the bodhisattva lives in society, drawing on the *Sigālaka Sūtra*, the Buddha's best-known teaching for householders. Fascicle 44 ends today.

"Towards those they have gathered in, sick or well, they never abandon them." "Towards known and unknown alike, equal regard." Venerable Miào Jìng: a friend has affection, and wisdom within the affection.
They become a refuge for those with no support, "never inventing a pretext to cause grief", and release resentment even towards those who have wronged them.

Avoid fourteen tainted deeds: the four root wrongs (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying); four causes of a waning reputation; six ways a fortune drains away. The treatise simply says "as stated in the *Sigālaka Sūtra*". In that sūtra, the young Sigālaka worships the six directions, and the Buddha turns them into relationships: parents to the east, teachers south, spouse and children west, friends north, servants and workers below, renunciants above, each with duties running both ways (a husband treats his wife with courtesy; an employer assigns work fitted to a worker's strength). Master Cháng Bǎi and Venerable Miào Jìng both explain it this way.

"Living within one's income" (Venerable Miào Jìng). "Whatever is entrusted to them can be relied on"; borrowing, "they never renege"; Master Cháng Bǎi: never cheating a seller who doesn't know the value of what they sell. A ruler governs by Dharma, not force. And the eight noble words: saying "seen" only for what was seen.

Veneration, spiritual friends, compassion, and knowledge of the world. It moves from the most devotional (offering to the Buddha) to the most practical (paying debts), and the treatise treats both as the same path. Fascicle 45 continues the factors of awakening.

quiz.q: "Known or unknown, an equal mind; as friend and companion." How do the lectures explain "péng" and "yǒu"?
options: Miào Jìng: yǒu is affection, péng wisdom within it; Cháng Bǎi: caring for each other, illuminating one another with shared light
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "yǒu" is affection — keeping good feeling; "péng" is wisdom — wisdom within the affection, unlike ordinary friendship. Master Cháng Bǎi: caring for one another as friends, lighting each other with shared brightness.

quiz.q: "The hidden six directions" is rendered "properly attend to the six directions." How do the lectures read "hidden"?
options: from the Sigālaka sūtra — bowing to six directions hides a meaning: parents, teachers, and other relations; the English loses this "hidden" sense
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: this is the teaching of the Sigālaka sūtra. Venerable Miào Jìng: the six directions are turned into parents, teachers, and so on — bowing to them that way is meaningful. "Hidden" means the Buddha used the custom to convey a concealed meaning; the English "properly attend" drops it.

quiz.q: The treatise says the fourteen tainted deeds are "as in the Sigālaka sūtra." How do the lectures count fourteen?
options: four wrong deeds, four bad causes, six ways of losing wealth — 4 + 4 + 6
quiz.why: "All of this should be understood exactly as stated in the Sigālaka sūtra." Master Cháng Bǎi: four wrong deeds of body and speech, four bad causes, and six ways of squandering wealth. Venerable Miào Jìng: two sets of four make eight, plus six faults make fourteen.

quiz.q: How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain "sustaining livelihood in balanced measure"?
options: spending within one's income — spending beyond means is unbalanced
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: it means living within one's income — spending more than you have is unbalanced. Master Cháng Bǎi: this concerns lay bodhisattvas' present self-benefit.

quiz.q: "A recognised treasure, the seller unaware — paying the true price, not shorting a fraction." What do the lectures say?
options: never cheating the unknowing seller of even a fraction — Miào Jìng: not even a little, let alone more
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: never cheating a seller who does not recognise the treasure — not letting them lose the smallest fraction. Venerable Miào Jìng: not deceiving them even a little, let alone more.

quiz.q: What are the "eight kinds of noble speech"?
options: saying seen, heard, sensed, known when so, and not seen, not heard, not sensed, not known when not
quiz.why: When asked about what they saw, they say they saw; likewise for heard, sensed, known; and when they did not see, hear, sense, or know, they say so. Venerable Miào Jìng: if he saw it, he says he saw it.

quiz.q: The closing phrase "enacting conduct in the world as it should be enacted" — how do the lectures explain it?
options: both agree: meeting beings honestly, respectfully, without arrogance
both: turning the wheel of dharma
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: always honest, respectful, free of arrogance in meeting beings. Master Cháng Bǎi: correctly, sincerely, respectfully, without pride — that is "as it should be enacted."
